events.title: Paul's voyage, shipwreck on Malta and house arrest in Rome
events.summary: Sent to Rome under guard of the centurion Julius, Paul sailed in an Alexandrian grain ship that was wrecked on Malta after a fourteen-day storm, c. 59-60; after wintering there he reached Rome, where Acts leaves him living two years under house arrest, preaching openly.
events.detail: The "we" narrative of Acts 27 is one of the most detailed accounts of an ancient voyage, with its sounding of depths, the anchoring by the stern and the 276 people aboard; James Smith's classic study (1848) showed its nautical plausibility. Acts says nothing of Paul's trial or death, a silence variously explained. The Pastoral letters and 1 Clement 5 ("he reached the limits of the west") gave rise to the tradition of release and a mission to Spain.

events.title: Revolt of Clodius Macer in Africa
events.summary: In 68 Lucius Clodius Macer, legate of the African legion, rebelled against Nero, raised a second legion (I Macriana Liberatrix), cut off Rome's grain supply from Africa and struck denarii without an emperor's portrait in the name of the Senate and Roman people; Galba had him killed by the procurator Trebonius Garutianus in autumn 68.
events.detail: Macer's coins, with legends such as L CLODI MACRI LIBERA(TRIX) and the S C on silver, are among the rarest and most sought-after of the period and show a programme of senatorial "liberation" without claiming the purple. Plutarch says Calvia Crispinilla, Nero's former mistress of the wardrobe, urged him to starve Rome.

events.title: The first false Nero
events.summary: Early in 69 a man resembling Nero, a slave from Pontus or a freedman from Italy who sang to the lyre, gathered deserters and sailors on the island of Cythnos until Calpurnius Asprenas, governor of Galatia and Pamphylia, captured and executed him and sent his head to Rome.
events.detail: Two further pretenders appeared: one under Titus (c. 80, Terentius Maximus, who found support in Parthia) and one c. 88, whom the Parthians nearly refused to surrender. The belief that Nero had not died or would return from the East (Nero redivivus) also shaped Jewish and Christian apocalyptic literature, including the Sibylline Oracles and possibly Revelation 13 and 17.

events.title: Revolt of Mariccus among the Boii
events.summary: In 69 Mariccus, a Boian of humble birth, proclaimed himself a god and liberator of Gaul and gathered 8,000 followers, raiding Aeduan villages; the Aedui and Vitellian cohorts crushed them, and Mariccus was thrown to the beasts, which refused to touch him until he was killed in front of Vitellius.
events.detail: Tacitus treats the movement as a symptom of the disorder of 69, comparable to the Druidic prophecies that the burning of the Capitol foretold the transfer of empire to the Transalpine peoples. It foreshadows the Gallic risings around Civilis and Classicus in 70.

events.title: Venutius overthrows Cartimandua
events.summary: Taking advantage of the civil war, Venutius, the divorced husband of the Brigantian queen Cartimandua, who had married his armour-bearer Vellocatus, raised the Brigantes against her in 69; Roman auxiliaries under Vettius Bolanus could only rescue the queen, leaving "the kingdom to Venutius, the war to us".
events.detail: Cartimandua had ruled northern England as a Roman client since the 40s and had surrendered Caratacus. Roman troops had already intervened in the couple's quarrels under Didius Gallus (c. 57). The loss of the client kingdom forced conquest: Petillius Cerialis campaigned against the Brigantes from 71, and the great hillfort at Stanwick may have been Venutius's base.

events.title: Vespasian's miracles at Alexandria
events.summary: Waiting at Alexandria in early 70 for the grain season and news from Rome, Vespasian was persuaded to heal a blind man by spitting in his eyes and a lame man by touching him with his foot, both on the advice of Serapis; visiting the Serapeum alone, he saw the absent Egyptian priest Basilides.
events.detail: Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio all report the miracles, which gave the new, low-born emperor the divine sanction he lacked. Tacitus says eyewitnesses still affirmed them when there was nothing to gain by lying. The Alexandrian crowd also hailed him as son of Ammon, as they had Alexander, and the Flavians promoted Egyptian cults at Rome (the Iseum Campense was rebuilt by Domitian).

events.title: Yohanan ben Zakkai and the academy at Yavneh
events.summary: According to rabbinic tradition the sage Yohanan ben Zakkai escaped besieged Jerusalem hidden in a coffin and obtained from Vespasian permission to found a school at Yavneh (Jamnia), where the rabbinic reconstruction of Judaism without a Temple began.
events.detail: The story (Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Babylonian Talmud Gittin 56a-b, Lamentations Rabbah) has Yohanan predict Vespasian's accession, echoing Josephus's claim to have done the same. Yavneh, where the Romans had interned loyalist Jews, became the seat of a court under Gamaliel II, which standardised liturgy and the calendar and debated the canon. The later picture of a "Council of Jamnia" that fixed the Hebrew Bible and expelled Christians is now largely rejected.
events.debate: The escape story is legendary; the importance of Yavneh is historical but the notion of a canon-fixing "council" is doubted.

events.title: The Gospel of Mark written
events.summary: The earliest gospel, attributed to Mark, was written about 66-72, probably in the shadow of the Jewish war and the destruction of the Temple, and became the narrative framework used by Matthew and Luke.
events.detail: Papias (c. 120, in Eusebius) says Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down what he remembered "but not in order". Mark 13, with its "abomination of desolation" and warnings to flee to the mountains, is usually read as reflecting 66-70. Place of writing is disputed between Rome (patristic tradition, Latinisms, persecution theme) and Syria or Galilee. The original text ends abruptly at 16.8 with the women fleeing the empty tomb; longer endings were added later.
events.debate: Date (before or after 70) and place (Rome, Syria, Galilee).

events.title: Vespasian settles veterans at Emmaus and leases Judaea
events.summary: After the war Vespasian treated Judaea as his own property, ordering the land to be leased out rather than founding a city, settling only 800 veterans at Emmaus 30 stades from Jerusalem, and imposing the two-drachma fiscus Judaicus on all Jews.
events.detail: Josephus says Lucilius Bassus received instructions to lease the land. The legion X Fretensis remained encamped on the ruins of Jerusalem, and the province was upgraded to a praetorian legateship with its own legion, governed from Caesarea, which became Colonia Prima Flavia Augusta. Flavia Neapolis was founded in Samaria in 72.

events.title: Censorship of Vespasian and Titus
events.summary: In 73-74 Vespasian and Titus held the censorship, revising the Senate and equestrian order after the civil wars, adlecting new members from Italy and the provinces into the Senate and the patriciate, conducting a census and extending the pomerium (75).
events.detail: Among those adlected to the patriciate were Agricola and the father of Trajan; Suetonius says Vespasian raised the orders to a thousand members from the best men of Italy and the provinces. The census returns gave Pliny the Elder his list of long-lived men in Region VIII. Pomerial cippi of 75 survive. This was the last formal censorship; Domitian took the title censor perpetuus in 85.

events.title: Vespasian's tax on urine and fiscal recovery
events.summary: To restore finances after the civil wars, which he said required 40 billion sesterces, Vespasian raised provincial tribute, revived lapsed taxes and imposed new ones, including a levy on the urine collected from public latrines by fullers; when Titus objected he held a coin to his nose and said "it doesn't smell" (non olet).
events.detail: Suetonius and Dio report his reputation for avarice, including selling offices and buying goods to resell. He also reclaimed public land (subseciva) occupied illegally in Italy, a policy Domitian reversed. In French and Italian, public urinals are still called vespasiennes and vespasiani.
events.debate: Date of the urine tax within the reign unknown.

events.title: Frontinus conquers the Silures
events.summary: Sextus Julius Frontinus, governor of Britain c. 74-77, subdued the warlike Silures of South Wales after decades of resistance, founding the legionary fortress of Isca (Caerleon) for II Augusta and a network of auxiliary forts.
events.detail: Tacitus (Agricola 17) says Frontinus "sustained the burden" worthily, overcoming the valour of the enemy and the difficulty of the ground. Frontinus later wrote the Strategemata and, as curator of the water supply, De Aquaeductu. The fortress at Caerleon, with its amphitheatre and baths, remained the base of II Augusta until the late third century.

events.title: Alan invasion of Media and Armenia
events.summary: Around 72-75 the Alans poured through the Caucasus passes, opened to them by the king of Hyrcania, plundering Media Atropatene, whose king Pacorus fled to the mountains, and Armenia, where Tiridates was nearly lassoed in battle; Vologases I asked Vespasian for help under Titus or Domitian, which was refused.
events.detail: Josephus describes the Alan raid; Suetonius says Vespasian refused Vologases's request. Rome instead strengthened the Caucasus: a Latin inscription of 75 at Harmozica near Tbilisi records Roman fortification work for the Iberian king Mithridates. The episode explains the Flavian reorganisation of the eastern frontier and the Alan threat that Arrian faced in 135.

events.title: Agricola crushes the Ordovices and takes Anglesey
events.summary: Arriving in Britain in midsummer (77 or 78), Agricola at once attacked the Ordovices, who had nearly wiped out a cavalry unit, slaughtered almost the whole tribe, and then took Mona by sending auxiliaries trained to swim with their horses across the Menai Strait.
events.detail: Tacitus (Agricola 18) stresses that Agricola campaigned when the season was thought over. The completion of the conquest of Wales freed forces for the advance north. The date of Agricola's arrival (77 or 78) determines all later years of his governorship and the date of Mons Graupius (83 or 84).

events.title: Agricola's "civilising" programme
events.summary: In his second winter Agricola encouraged British communities to build temples, forums and houses, educated chiefs' sons in the liberal arts and promoted Latin and the toga, a policy Tacitus famously describes as the Britons calling "civilisation" (humanitas) what was in fact part of their enslavement.
events.detail: Agricola 21 is the classic text on "Romanisation". The forum at Verulamium, dedicated under Agricola in 79 according to a fragmentary inscription, and the early masonry phases of Fishbourne and other towns illustrate the building boom. Modern scholarship debates how far Roman officials drove such change rather than local elites seeking status.
events.debate: Romanisation as policy or as elite emulation (Haverfield, Millett, Woolf).

events.title: Agricola advances to the Tay
events.summary: In his third season Agricola overran new peoples as far as the estuary called Taus (the Tay), ravaging as he went, and built forts so well sited that none was stormed or abandoned.
events.detail: Tacitus says the garrisons were supplied for a year and could survive winter sieges. Dendrochronology and coin evidence support Flavian occupation of Scotland in this period, though many of the forts in Strathmore may belong to the following years.

events.title: Agricola garrisons the Forth-Clyde isthmus
events.summary: In his fourth season Agricola consolidated the land he had overrun and fortified the narrow neck between the Clota (Clyde) and Bodotria (Forth), so that the enemy were "pushed back as if into another island".
events.detail: Tacitus remarks that if the army's valour and Rome's glory had allowed, a frontier could have been found within Britain itself. The same isthmus was later chosen for the Antonine Wall (142).

events.title: Agricola in south-west Scotland and the Irish question
events.summary: In his fifth season Agricola crossed by ship (or the Solway) and subdued previously unknown peoples in the south-west, placing troops facing Ireland; he believed Ireland could be conquered and held with one legion and a modest force of auxiliaries, and kept an exiled Irish prince in his entourage.
events.detail: Tacitus says he often heard Agricola say this. No Roman conquest of Ireland followed; finds at Drumanagh north of Dublin and elsewhere attest trade rather than occupation. The passage is the earliest Roman reference to Irish harbours being known through merchants.
events.locName: Galloway and the coast facing Ireland

events.title: The Usipi cohort mutinies and sails round Britain
events.summary: In 82 or 83 a cohort of Usipi recruited in Germany and posted to Britain murdered their centurion and drill instructors, seized three liburnian galleys and sailed round the north of Britain, reduced by hunger to cannibalism, until they were shipwrecked and enslaved by the Suebi and Frisii, some being sold back across the Rhine.
events.detail: Tacitus (Agricola 28) tells the story as an unintended circumnavigation that preceded Agricola's own fleet. Dio (66.20) has a garbled version making the mutineers prove Britain an island. The episode illustrates the risks of using newly levied German auxiliaries far from home.

events.title: Fire of 80 and pestilence under Titus
events.summary: A three-day fire in 80, while Titus was in Campania dealing with the aftermath of Vesuvius, destroyed the newly rebuilt Capitoline temple, the Pantheon, the Saepta, the Baths of Agrippa, the Theatre of Balbus and the stage of Pompey's theatre; a severe epidemic followed.
events.detail: Titus stripped his own villas of decorations to restore public buildings and appointed two ex-consuls to relieve Campania, using the estates of those who died without heirs. Domitian rebuilt the Capitol on a lavish scale (gilding alone reputedly cost 12,000 talents) and restored the Pantheon. The fire and epidemic gave Titus's short reign its reputation for disaster borne with generosity.

events.title: Arch of Titus on the Sacra Via
events.summary: After Titus's death in September 81 the Senate dedicated to Divus Titus a single-bay marble arch at the top of the Sacra Via, whose reliefs show the triumph of 71 with the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple, including the seven-branched menorah, the table of shewbread and silver trumpets.
events.detail: The vault shows Titus carried to heaven by an eagle, a key image of imperial apotheosis. A second, triple arch to Titus in the Circus Maximus (dedicated in 81 while he lived) claimed he had subdued the Jews and destroyed Jerusalem, "never before attacked", a falsehood. The surviving arch was built into the Frangipani fortress and restored by Valadier in 1821, who marked his additions in travertine. The menorah relief became a symbol of the Jewish diaspora.

events.title: Titus sends Berenice away
events.summary: The Jewish queen Berenice, sister of Agrippa II, came to Rome in 75 and lived with Titus on the Palatine expecting marriage, but popular hostility forced him to send her away, finally on his accession in 79: "invitus invitam" as Suetonius puts it.
events.detail: Two Cynic philosophers who denounced her in the theatre were punished, one by flogging and one by beheading (Dio). Berenice, born in 28, had been married to her uncle Herod of Chalcis and to Polemon of Cilicia, and had tried to calm the Jerusalem crowd barefoot in 66. The episode, with its echo of Antony and Cleopatra, inspired Racine's Berenice (1670).

events.title: Domitian becomes censor for life
events.summary: In 85 Domitian took the title censor perpetuus, giving himself permanent control over the membership of the Senate and equestrian order and over public morals, which he exercised by reviving the adultery law, expelling a quaestorian senator for acting and dancing, and punishing Vestals.
events.detail: The title appears on coins from 85 (CENS PER P). Dio says he was the first to hold it for life. His moral censorship included forbidding castration, enforcing the Lex Scantinia against homosexual acts among the elite and banning women of ill-repute from inheritances. The execution of the chief Vestal Cornelia (91) was its most notorious act.

events.title: Revolt and destruction of the Nasamones
events.summary: In 85-86 the Nasamones of the Syrtic desert, crushed by taxation, killed the tax collectors and defeated the legate of Numidia, Gnaeus Suellius Flaccus, plundering his camp; finding wine there, they got drunk and Flaccus fell on them and wiped them out, women and children included.
events.detail: Dio says Domitian boasted to the Senate: "I have forbidden the Nasamones to exist." Inscriptions of Flaccus record a census of the Nybgenii and the measurement of lands in southern Tunisia. The episode shows the pressure of taxation on peripheral peoples and the brutality of frontier warfare.

events.title: Domitian founds the Capitoline Games
events.summary: In 86 Domitian instituted the Agon Capitolinus in honour of Jupiter Capitolinus, a quadrennial Greek-style festival of music, horsemanship and athletics, with oak-leaf crowns presented by the emperor wearing a Greek cloak and gold crown with images of the Capitoline triad.
events.detail: For it he built the Stadium (whose outline survives as the Piazza Navona) and the Odeum. The poet Statius failed to win the crown in 90, a disappointment he lamented. The Capitoline Games, unlike Nero's Neronia, endured into the fourth century and became one of the most prestigious contests in the Greek athletic circuit; the eleven-year-old poet Quintus Sulpicius Maximus is commemorated on his tomb near the Porta Salaria for his Greek improvisation at the 94 games.
events.locName: Stadium and Odeum of Domitian, Campus Martius

events.title: Moesia divided into two provinces
events.summary: After the Dacian invasion that killed Oppius Sabinus, Domitian divided Moesia in 86 into Moesia Superior (capital Viminacium) and Moesia Inferior (Novae), each with its own consular legate and legions, as the Danube became the empire's main front.
events.detail: The two Germanies had been organised as formal provinces with civil governors around the same time (c. 83-85). The concentration of legions on the Danube, which rose from about seven under Vespasian to twelve under Trajan, reflected the end of expansion on the Rhine and the rise of Dacia.

events.title: Upper and Lower Germany become provinces; the Taunus-Wetterau limes
events.summary: After his Chattan war (83) Domitian annexed the Taunus and Wetterau, building a line of forts and watchtowers linked by a patrol road, and organised the military zones on the Rhine as the provinces of Germania Superior and Inferior, governed from Mogontiacum and Colonia Agrippinensis.
events.detail: Frontinus (Strategemata 1.3.10) describes Domitian driving roads 120 miles long through the forest to expose the enemy's hiding places. The Agri Decumates between upper Rhine and Danube were gradually occupied in the same period. Military diplomas from 90 first name Germania Superior. The palisade and later rampart and ditch that made the Upper German-Raetian limes a continuous barrier were added under Hadrian and the Antonines.

events.title: Septimius Flaccus and Julius Maternus reach Agisymba
events.summary: In the Flavian period Septimius Flaccus marched three months south of the Garamantes, and Julius Maternus travelled with the Garamantian king four months from Garama to Agisymba, "the land of the Ethiopians where the rhinoceros gathers".
events.detail: The expeditions are known only from Marinus of Tyre as cited and criticised by Ptolemy (Geography 1.8), who doubted the distances. Agisymba has been located anywhere from the Tibesti to Lake Chad. The journeys reflect good relations with the Garamantes after the punitive expedition of Valerius Festus in 69-70 and the trade route to the Fezzan.

events.title: Domitian styled dominus et deus
events.summary: Suetonius says Domitian dictated a circular letter in the name of "our lord and god" (dominus et deus noster) and that the formula became usual in speech and writing addressed to him; Martial uses it in his epigrams.
events.detail: The phrase never appears in official documents or on coins, and some scholars think the hostile tradition exaggerated a courtiers' flattery into imperial policy. Martial, after Domitian's death, declared (10.72) that under Trajan there would be no more "lord and god". Domitian's favouring of Minerva and the cult of the Flavian gens was nevertheless distinctive.
events.debate: Whether Domitian demanded the title or flatterers used it.

events.title: Martial's epigrams
events.summary: Marcus Valerius Martialis of Bilbilis published the Liber Spectaculorum for the inaugural games of the Colosseum in 80, the Xenia and Apophoreta (84-85), and then twelve books of Epigrams from 86 to 101, the definitive models of the genre.
events.detail: His 1,500 poems are a street-level chronicle of Rome: legacy hunters, dinner parties, bath-houses, booksellers in the Argiletum, the clients' morning salutation, gladiators and the poet's own poverty in a third-floor flat. They flatter Domitian lavishly; after 96 Martial courted Nerva and Trajan with less success and retired to Bilbilis in 98, where he died c. 102-104. Pliny paid his travel money and wrote his obituary.

events.title: Lex Irnitana: the Flavian municipal law
events.summary: Bronze tablets discovered in 1981 near El Saucejo (Seville) preserve about two-thirds of the charter of the small Baetican town of Irni, a model municipal law issued under Domitian (with a covering letter of 91) for the communities that received Latin rights from Vespasian.
events.detail: The law regulates the town council of 63 decurions, the annual magistrates (duoviri, aediles, quaestors) who gained Roman citizenship on taking office, elections, public finances, manumission, guardianship and civil jurisdiction, which followed Roman law and procedure even between Latin citizens. With the fragments from Malaca and Salpensa (found 1851) it shows how Rome built provincial self-government on a standard template.

events.title: Statius publishes the Thebaid
events.summary: Publius Papinius Statius of Naples published the Thebaid, a twelve-book epic on the war of the Seven against Thebes, around 91-92, after twelve years' work; his Silvae, occasional poems on villas, statues, baths and court life, followed in 92-95.
events.detail: The Thebaid ends by telling the poem not to rival "the divine Aeneid" but to follow it at a distance. Statius won the prize at Domitian's Alban games but lost at the Capitoline. Dante, who believed him a secret Christian, made him his guide in Purgatory. The Silvae include the poem on Domitian's colossal equestrian statue in the Forum and the poem to Sleep.

events.title: Josephus completes the Jewish Antiquities
events.summary: In the thirteenth year of Domitian (93/94) Josephus completed the twenty books of the Jewish Antiquities, a history of the Jews from the creation to the outbreak of the revolt, followed by his autobiography (Life) and Against Apion, a defence of Judaism against Greek slanders.
events.detail: The Antiquities paraphrases the Bible and adds post-biblical sources (Nicolaus of Damascus, Hellenistic Jewish writers, Roman decrees). Book 18 contains the notices of John the Baptist, James and the much-debated Testimonium Flavianum on Jesus, which made Josephus a favourite of Christian copyists and ensured his survival. The patron was Epaphroditus, possibly not Nero's freedman of that name.

events.title: Epictetus founds his school at Nicopolis
events.summary: Expelled from Rome with the other philosophers in 93 (or 89), the former slave Epictetus set up a Stoic school at Nicopolis in Epirus, where young Romans and Greeks came to study; Arrian's notes of his lectures, the Discourses and the Handbook (Enchiridion), are the most vivid record of ancient philosophical teaching.
events.detail: Epictetus had been a slave of Nero's freedman Epaphroditus and was lame. His teaching centred on distinguishing what is "up to us" (judgements, desires) from what is not. Hadrian reportedly visited him, and Marcus Aurelius read the Discourses, lent to him by Junius Rusticus.

events.title: Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria
events.summary: Marcus Fabius Quintilianus of Calagurris, the first holder of a state-salaried chair of Latin rhetoric (founded by Vespasian, 100,000 sesterces a year), published his twelve-book Education of the Orator c. 95, a complete programme from infancy to the mature speaker.
events.detail: Book 10 contains a reading list surveying Greek and Latin literature with famous verdicts ("satura quidem tota nostra est"). Quintilian taught Pliny the Younger and was tutor to Domitian's grand-nephews, the sons of Flavius Clemens, for which he received the consular insignia. The rediscovery of a complete manuscript by Poggio Bracciolini at St Gall in 1416 made him central to Renaissance humanist education.

events.title: The Revelation of John
events.summary: The Apocalypse of John, written by a Christian prophet exiled on Patmos, is dated by Irenaeus to the end of Domitian's reign (c. 95), though some place it c. 68-70; its seven letters address churches in Asia, and its visions present Rome as Babylon and the beast.
events.detail: The number of the beast, 666 (616 in some manuscripts), is most commonly read as a gematria of "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters, and the wounded head that revives as a reflection of the Nero redivivus legend. The book's picture of Domitianic persecution is not confirmed by other evidence; it more likely reflects pressures of the imperial cult in Asia. It was admitted to the canon only after long dispute in the East.
events.debate: Date (Neronian or Domitianic) and the reality of a Domitianic persecution.

events.title: Letter of the Roman church to Corinth (1 Clement)
events.summary: Around 96 the church of Rome, through its leading presbyter Clement, wrote to the Corinthians urging the reinstatement of presbyters deposed by younger members, the earliest Christian text outside the New Testament.
events.detail: The letter apologises for delay caused by "sudden and repeated misfortunes", often taken as Domitianic pressure. It contains the first reference to the deaths of Peter and Paul and an early statement of apostolic succession of church officers. Later lists made Clement the third or fourth bishop of Rome, but the letter itself suggests government by a college of presbyters.

events.title: The later gospels and Acts
events.summary: Between about 80 and 100 the gospels of Matthew and Luke, both using Mark and a common sayings source (Q), and Luke's sequel Acts, were written for Greek-speaking communities; the Gospel of John, independent in structure and theology, followed c. 90-100, traditionally at Ephesus.
events.detail: Matthew, possibly from Antioch, frames Jesus as interpreter of the Law and reflects a community in conflict with the emerging rabbinic leadership. Luke-Acts is addressed to the "most excellent Theophilus" and tells a story from Galilee to Rome. John speaks of believers being "put out of the synagogue". The Rylands papyrus P52, a fragment of John often dated c. 125-175, is among the earliest New Testament manuscripts.
events.debate: Dates, places and the Q hypothesis (two-source theory versus Farrer-Goulder) are all debated.

events.title: Nerva's reforms: land law and the end of informers
events.summary: In his brief reign Nerva recalled exiles, banned prosecutions for maiestas and "Jewish living", executed informing slaves and freedmen, passed an agrarian law spending 60 million sesterces on land for poor citizens and exempted Italy from the cost of the imperial post.
events.detail: His coins advertise FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA (the abuse of the Jewish tax removed), VEHICVLATIONE ITALIAE REMISSA and PLEBEI VRBANAE FRUMENTO CONSTITVTO. Economies included selling imperial property. The consul Fronto remarked that it was bad to have an emperor under whom nothing was allowed, but worse to have one under whom everything was. The alimentary schemes probably began under him.

events.title: Nerva dedicates the Forum Transitorium
events.summary: In 97 Nerva dedicated the narrow forum built by Domitian between the Forum of Augustus and the Temple of Peace, along the line of the Argiletum, with a temple of Minerva, Domitian's patron goddess.
events.detail: The forum's frieze of the "Colonnacce" shows Minerva and scenes of women's work (the myth of Arachne). The temple survived largely intact until Pope Paul V dismantled it in 1606 for the Acqua Paola fountain. Domitian's name was erased and Nerva's substituted, a typical case of the appropriation of a condemned emperor's building.

events.title: Frontinus becomes water commissioner and writes De Aquaeductu
events.summary: Appointed curator aquarum by Nerva in 97, the elderly Frontinus surveyed Rome's nine aqueducts, found widespread fraud by water-men and landowners tapping the conduits, and wrote On the Aqueducts of Rome, with figures for each channel's source, length and delivery.
events.detail: He found that the official delivery figures underestimated actual intake and that much water was stolen by illegal pipes and wrongly sized nozzles (calices). He praises the aqueducts over "idle pyramids" and the "famous but useless works of the Greeks". Frontinus was consul for the third time in 100 with Trajan.

events.title: Tacitus publishes the Agricola and Germania
events.summary: In 98 Tacitus published his biography of his father-in-law Agricola and his ethnographic treatise on the peoples of Germany, his first works after the "fifteen years" of silence under Domitian.
events.detail: The Agricola's preface celebrates the return of liberty under Nerva and Trajan and contains Calgacus's speech at Mons Graupius ("they make a desert and call it peace"). The Germania, contrasting German virtue with Roman decadence, survived in a single manuscript found at Hersfeld and brought to Rome in 1455; it was later abused by German nationalists and the Nazis. Tacitus had been consul suffect in 97 and delivered the funeral oration for Verginius Rufus.
